body:
Point 1

> 16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and time zone. Strongly consider logging only in UTC if systems are global to assist with post-incident forensic analysis.

"Strongly consider logging only in UTC if systems are global to assist with post-incident forensic analysis."

Change this part to something like:
> It is recommended to use UTC to assist with post-incident forensic analysis for logs from global systems and daylight saving time switches.

---

Point 2

> 16.2.5 Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application considers the protection level of the data. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data such as credentials or payment details. Other data such as session tokens may only be logged having been hashed or masked, either in full or partially.

Nothing to consider, it must be applied.

The last part requires some work as well, but I have not changed it.

> 16.2.5 Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application applies the defence based on the protection level of the data. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged having been hashed or masked, either in full or partially.

---

Point 3

16.3.1

grammar updates:
> Verify that all authentication operations are logged, including both successful and unsuccessful attempts. Additional metadata, such as the type of authentication or factors used, should also be collected.

---

Point 4

> 16.3.5 Verify that accessing sensitive data is logged (without logging the sensitive data itself) if this is required by relevant data protection requirements.

Is it covered by 16.3.2? Or it requires some special attention?

---

Point 5

> 16.4.3 Verify that logs are securely transmitted to a logically separate system for analysis, detection, alerting, and escalation. The aim is to ensure that if the application is breached, the logs are not also compromised.

remove "also"

---

Point 6

> 16.5.1 Verify that a generic message is shown when an unexpected or security sensitive error occurs, which does not expose sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.

"is shown" - can be more precise and clear - to whom by whom

---

Point 7

> 16.5.2 Verify that the application is designed in a way that a failure to access external resources does not result in the entire application failing, for example using the circuit breaker pattern.

Should we ask to verify design or how it works in practice?

The message (but requires to be written to positive requirement), pattern from 16.5.3 can be used.
> 16.5.2 Verify that a failure to access external resources does not result in the entire application failing, for example using the circuit breaker pattern.

comments.body:
Nice. I'd suggest for 16.2.2:

_16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and time zone. It is recommended to use UTC to assist with post-incident forensic analysis, especially for logs from global systems and environments affected by daylight saving time changes._

Suggestion based on Elar's comments:

_16.2.5 Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data’s sensitivity level. For example, credentials or payment details must not be logged. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged if they are securely hashed or masked._
16.3.5  looks like a duplicate and I think it can go away.

Suggestion to make 16.5.2 positive:

_16.5.2 Verify that the application continues to operate securely when external resource access fails, for example by using patterns such as circuit breakers or graceful degradation._
The rest of you comments on 16.x look good to me.

> 16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and time zone. It is recommended to use UTC to assist with post-incident forensic analysis, especially for logs from global systems and environments affected by daylight saving time changes.

"synchronized […] to the correct time zone" is weird? I'd better say:

> Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and configured to the correct time zone.

On the other hand, the part about the time zone in the first sentence is weird. From the context "General Logging", it can be understood that the "time zone" part is about *producing logs* but this is not explicitly stated. The requirement should have its meaning in isolation of its context. In order to do that, shall we instead say:

> 16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and that logs are produced using the correct time zone.

Even then "the correct time zone" is somewhat vague. What is "the" correct time zone? (It appears the correct time zone should be UTC 😄). As an alternative to "produced using the correct time zone", would it be OK to just include the time offset in the logs?

Shall we instead say:

> 16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and that there is no ambiguity about when the logged events occurred. When using a human-oriented format for event times, it is recommended to include the time zone offset. It is recommended to use UTC to assist with post-incident forensic analysis, especially for logs from global systems and environments affected by daylight saving time changes.

Note: @randomstuff I edited this on accident and reverted to back to your original post, my apologies! It was not intentional.

> 16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and that there is no ambiguity about when the logged events occurred. When using a human-oriented format for event times, it is recommended to include the time zone offset. It is recommended to use UTC to assist with post-incident forensic analysis, especially for logs from global systems and environments affected by daylight saving time changes.

I think this is way better than earlier proposals including mine. I love it. If we want to make it a little less wordy, I would consider reducing it to:

_16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized and that logged events include unambiguous timestamps. When using human-readable formats, include the time zone offset and that UTC is used for consistency across distributed systems and to aid forensic analysis, especially in environments impacted by daylight saving time._

I think UTC is the most important element here. So maybe even this if we want to keep it brief:

_16.2.2 Verify that time sources are synchronized and that logged events use UTC for consistency across distributed systems and to aid forensic analysis, especially in environments impacted by daylight saving time._

* I think human-readable format is not something we need into the requirement
* We can not require UTC, we can only recommend it.

Proposal with combining previous ideas and statements above:
> Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized, and the time value in security event metadata contains information about the timezone. It is recommended to use UTC for consistency across distributed systems and to aid forensic analysis, especially in environments impacted by daylight saving time.

I like that one best @elarlang - just one tiny suggestion from my grammar checker.


_16.2.2 Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized, and that the time values in security event metadata include timezone information. It is recommended to use UTC for consistency across distributed systems and to aid in forensic analysis, especially in environments affected by daylight saving time._

> Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized, and the time value in security event metadata contains information about the timezone. It is recommended to use UTC for consistency across distributed systems and to aid forensic analysis, especially in environments impacted by daylight saving time.

Nitpick, if the time is stored as a Unix timestamp (number of seconds since Epoch), there is no notion of timezone: a Unix timestamp is supposed to represent a point in time and is the same for the same time across all the globe. I would say that information about the timezone is (mostly) only relevant when the information is stored in a human-friendly format.

So perhaps:

_16.2.2 Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized. It is recommended to use UTC for consistency across distributed systems and to aid in forensic analysis, especially in environments affected by daylight saving time._

Let's keep all the pointed out details in requirement.

> Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized, and the time value in security event metadata is in UTC or contains information about the timezone. UTC is recommended for consistency across distributed systems and avoiding confusion when switching daylight saving time.

> Verify that time sources for different logging components are synchronized, and the time value in security event metadata is in UTC or contains information about the timezone. UTC is recommended for consistency across distributed systems and avoiding confusion when switching daylight saving time

Sounds good, I would suggest one more grammar cleanup and use of more standard logging terminology for this one. But regardless,  I think we are all on the same page now and I appreciate all the time spend to clean this up! Hows this?

_16.2.2  Verify that time sources for all logging components are synchronized, and that timestamps in security event metadata use UTC or include an explicit timezone offset. UTC is recommended to ensure consistency across distributed systems and to prevent confusion during daylight saving time transitions._
I'm now waiting @randomstuff reaction on the word "timestamp"
My reasoning is, most logging frameworks and standards (ISO 8601, RFC 5424), and tools in the field use timestamp.
Yes, better aligning the wording with logging standards is a good move. 👍

Update. (Note that I had incorrect "Point numbers" in the issue and point numbers in commit messages may be incorrect, requirement numbers are correct)

Patch one PR #2989 - Done: Point 1, Point 3, Point 5, Point 7

---

Point 2 - done, but recheck

Last proposal:
> 16.2.5 Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's sensitivity level. For example, credentials or payment details must not be logged. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged if they are securely hashed or masked.

* "based on the data's sensitivity level" > "based on data's protection level"
* "For example, credentials or payment details must not be logged." - "may not be allowed to log" is changed to "must not" - we can not say that any payment detail can not be logged. It is just an example here that may not be allowed to log.
* "Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged if they are securely hashed or masked." - here I prefer the original version.

So I used at the moment combination of previous requirement and your proposal:
> Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's protection level. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data, such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged by being hashed or masked, either in full or partially.

---

Point 4 - @tghosth , please check do you agree that 16.3.5 is covered by 16.3.2?

* 16.3.2 Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3 this must include logging all authorization decisions.
* 16.3.5 Verify that accessing sensitive data is logged (without logging the sensitive data itself) if this is required by relevant data protection requirements.

---

Point 6 - requires further work

> 16.5.1 Verify that a generic message is shown when an unexpected or security sensitive error occurs, which does not expose sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.
> "is shown" - can be more precise and clear - to whom by whom

How about:

_16.5.1 Verify that a generic message is displayed to the user when an unexpected or security sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens._

> Point 4 - [@tghosth](https://github.com/tghosth) , please check do you agree that 16.3.5 is covered by 16.3.2?
> 
> * 16.3.2 Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3 this must include logging all authorization decisions.
> 
> * 16.3.5 Verify that accessing sensitive data is logged (without logging the sensitive data itself) if this is required by relevant data protection requirements.

Apologies for the delay, I think it requires a careful merge but yes I agree.

I would suggest:

"_16.3.2 Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3 this must include logging all authorization decisions, including logging when sensitive data is accessed (without logging the sensitive data itself)._"
Ack, I'll handle the PR later. It requires some mapping updates.

One is super important - logging access control failures.

One is way less important - logging when sensitive data was accessed legally.

We already have requirements that discuss rate limiting and similar to detect abusive access to sensitive data.

I question if logging sensitive data access is worth burying access control failure.

I'd be more comfortable with dropping "including logging when sensitive data is accessed (without logging the sensitive data itself)." I think the addition is confusing. So perhaps just:

"16.3.2 Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3 this must include logging all authorization decisions."
One more side note. The logging vocabulary cheat sheet that this section cites has the details I'm suggesting we remove.

> One is super important - logging access control failures.

This part is Level 2

> One is way less important - logging when sensitive data was accessed legally.

... and this part is Level 3.

> I question if logging sensitive data access is worth burying access control failure.

As one is L2 and another is L3, this concern is not justified in my opinion.

It means, I'll PR the version Josh proposed - keeping the sensitive data in text has the goal to highlight the problem with sensitive data, although technically it is covered by the first part of the requirement (that was also the reason why I said it is a duplicate or covered)

For Point 6, 16.5.1 I go with:

> 16.5.1 Verify that a generic message is displayed to the user when an unexpected or security sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.

Changed "a generic message is displayed to the user" to "a generic message is returned to the consumer"

> 16.5.1 Verify that a generic message is returned to the consumer when an unexpected or security-sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.
